t: Maximum Number of Accepted Invitations — Maximum Bipartite Matching
o:
**Understanding the problem**

Boy i may invite girl j only when grid[i][j] = 1; each boy sends at most one invitation and each girl accepts at most one. Maximizing accepted invitations is exactly **maximum bipartite matching**: boys on the left, girls on the right, an edge wherever grid[i][j] = 1. Example 1 admits a perfect matching of size 3 (boy 1 to girl 2, boy 2 to girl 1, boy 3 to girl 3). Example 2 answers 3: boy 1 takes girl 3, boy 2 girl 1, boy 4 girl 2, leaving boy 3 unmatched because every eligible girl is already taken. With m, n <= 200 the graph has about 400 nodes and at most 40,000 edges, so classic augmenting-path matching is more than fast enough.
k: One-to-one invitations under an eligibility matrix = maximum matching in a bipartite graph.
Greedy assignment fails: seating an early boy with a contested girl can strand a later boy who has no alternative — matchings must be repairable by rerouting.
An augmenting path alternates free and matched edges; flipping it grows the matching by one, and when none exists the matching is provably maximum (Berge lemma).

a.i: Decide boys one at a time: either leave a boy unmatched or pair him with any eligible girl who is currently free, undoing the choice on backtrack. Exploring every combination examines the whole space of matchings, so it is obviously correct — and hopelessly slow on large inputs, since branching explodes factorially.
s: Keep match[girl] = currently paired boy, or -1 if she is free.
Recurse over boys in order; at each boy try skipping him and pairing him with each eligible free girl.
Take the maximum count over the choices, undoing tentative pairs while backtracking.
Return the best value once all boys are decided.
a.t: Exponential — worst case it enumerates a factorial-size space of partial matchings; only viable for tiny inputs
a.sp: O(m + n) for recursion depth and the match array

a.i: Start unmatched. For each boy, launch a DFS hunting an augmenting path: a chain that seats this boy by walking through already-paired boys and asking each to relocate to another girl. A per-search visited flag guarantees each girl is examined once per DFS. Success means flipping every pair along the path, growing the matching by exactly one. Once every boy has been processed, no augmenting path remains, so by Berge lemma the matching is maximum.
s: Maintain match[girl]; run one DFS per boy.
Inside the DFS iterate girls j with grid[i][j] = 1 that are unvisited in the current search, marking j visited.
Girl j can seat boy i if she is free, or if her current partner match[j] can be relocated via a recursive DFS.
Add one to the answer for each successful boy; the total is the answer.
a.t: O(m^2 * n) — each of the m searches visits every girl once and scans at most all m*n edges; about 8 million steps at n = m = 200
a.sp: O(m + n) for the match array, visited flags and recursion stack

w:
**Wrap-up**

The decisive interview step is recognizing bipartite matching; implement the Kuhn DFS from muscle memory. Pitfalls: forgetting to reset the visited flags for every boy search, recursing on girls instead of the matched BOY (match[j] holds a boy index), and misreading the answer as invitations sent rather than accepted pairs. Iterating over the smaller side as the outer loop speeds the search. Follow-ups: Hopcroft-Karp improves this to O(E*sqrt(V)) for large graphs, and weighted preferences lead to the Hungarian algorithm or min-cost max-flow.
